#845. Knicks React After Player Tyler Kolek Calls Taylor Swift Fakest Fan

The New York Knicks came to the defense of Taylor Swift after the team's point guard Tyler Kolek admitted that he thought she was a fake fan: "It’s a little performative."

The New York Knicks are pledging allegiance to Taylor Swift.

Shortly after the NBA team’s point guard Tyler Kolek declared the Grammy winner as one of their fakest fans, the Knicks went on the defensive for the “Love Story” singer.

“Taylor Swift has been a Knicks fan for many years, has a long history with Madison Square Garden,” a spokesperson for the team said in a Nov. 6 statement to E! News, “and we are incredibly appreciative of her support of the organization.”

Kolek and his fellow point guard Miles James “Deuce” McBride found themselves in some trouble during an interview with NBA 2K League, when they were faced with the question: “Who’s the fakest celebrity fan you’ve seen sitting courtside in an NBA game?” And Kolek did his part to keep it 100 on the land, the sea, the sky—by calling out his perceived fair-weather fans.

“At the Knicks games, I would say it’s very performative,” Kolek mused in a video posted to YouTube Nov. 5, “like they just want to be seen at the game, they’re not necessarily fans.”

The 25-year-old, who is beginning his third season with the team, suggested that Swift wasn’t actually a big fan of the Knicks, noting that beyond seeing her at some playoff games, “I don’t know if I’ve seen her at any other games.”

And while McBride, 26, agreed with his teammate, he was a little nervous about the admission, saying, “Swifties not gonna like that answer.”

Doubling down with his qualms about her fandom aside, Kolek did concede that the “Fortnight” singer—who married Travis Kelce at the Knicks home court of Madison Square Garden July 3—does have quite a packed schedule. As he put it, “I guess she’s got a lot going on so she can’t come all the time, but it’s a little performative.”

Still, Swift—who has been photographed at several games over the years—was one of the most vocal supporters of the Knicks as they won the NBA championship earlier this year. In fact, she attended game four with friends Alana Haim, Este Haim and Mariksa Hargitay wearing punny custom New York Knicks merch, with Swift’s shirt reading “Stevie Knicks.”

The 36-year-old and Kelce also took on the role of cheer captain for the team during the May Eastern Conference finals in Cleveland, Ohio, with the Rocket Arena chair she sat later being put up for auction by The Realest and selling for $7,000.

Of course, this isn’t the first time Swift has faced questions of her Knicks fandom, with analyst Monica McNutt saying during the June 10 broadcast of the championship game, “Is that Taylor Swift down there? She’s not a Knicks fan. Get out of here girl.”

McNutt later apologized for misspeaking, telling TMZ in June, “Shoutout T-Swift. We can be united."

For more stars who’ve always lived the life of a Knicks fan, keep reading.

When it comes to Timothée Chalamet's fandoms, his love of the New York Knicks reigns supreme."My grandma was a huge Knicks fan, so that's what turned me onto them," the Marty Supreme star told 7PM in Brooklyn in 2025. "If you live in New York, you are a Knicks fan."

And if you've been keeping up, then you know Kylie Jenner has been joining Chalamet, whom she's dated since 2023, courtside to cheer on the Knicks.

You could never sever Ben Stiller's tie to the Knicks. In fact, the Severance director said that if he could choose between winning an Oscar or having the team take the championship title, he'd pick the latter."I really think, at the end of the day, if I knew that I had the choice, I would give it to the Knicks," he said on New Heights in 2025, "because I knew at least I had the choice in this weird, non-real situation."

Spike Lee is a longtime Knicks superfan and believes the 2025-2026 roster has what it takes to secure the trophy."I don’t care about San Antonio. OKC,” the filmmaker told the New York Post in May 2026. “We’re going to win.”

Nothing could rock Tracy Morgan's love for the Knicks. As the 30 Rock alum put it on The Rich Eisen Show in 2021, "I'm the biggest Knicks fan there is besides Spike."

Live from New York...it's Pete Davidson. The Saturday Night Live alum has often been seen sitting courtside.

Chris Rock's loyalty to the Knicks is no laughing matter as the comedian has attended many games over the years.

Larry David isn't going to curb his enthusiasm for the Knicks.

And neither is his costar JB Smoove."How it started vs How it ended," the actor wrote on Instagram in 2024. "It’ll always be Knicks for life."

Jordyn Woods' love for the Knicks extends on and off the court. The Woods by Jordyn founder is engaged to the team's center Karl-Anthony Towns.

While Cardi B has a song called "Bodak Yellow," she's all about that orange and blue. In fact, the rapper and former Patriots player Stefon Diggs officially debuted their romance at a 2025 game between the Knicks and the Boston Celtics.

Is Anne Hathaway wearing the  Chanel boots Knicks colors? Yeah, she is. The Devil Wears Prada star showed where her loyalties lie by donning an orange and blue pocket square to The Tonight Show in April 2026.

"I’m very chill," she told host Jimmy Fallon about her fandom. "I’m very loving and calm. But I’m also the type of fan that I considered wearing an OG jersey out here today."

Speaking of which, Fallon is also a big fan of the Knicks, with him even bringing his eldest daughter Franny along for the ride during the 2026 NBA playoffs.

You don't have to travel back to the future to see how much Michael J. Fox loves the Knicks. The actor has gone to many games with his wife Tracy Pollan.

Throughout the Knicks' ups and downs, Jon Stewart has continued to support the team, with The Daily Show host calling himself a "ride or die" fan.

A Knicks win is music to Maggie Rogers' ears as the singer has documented her love for the organization.

#843. 'Bruno's as good as ever' - Carrick backs Man Utd captain

Bruno Fernandes' penalty sparked Manchester United's second-half revival against Roma in the Champions League

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick says captain Bruno Fernandes' commitment to the club is "undoubted" and the midfielder is "as good as ever".

Fernandes was left on the bench for October's home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick and his coaching staff in the wake of the 4-1 Champions League hammering in Como.

Restored to the team for the Premier League defeat by Chelsea a week later, Fernandes scored a retaken penalty to spark his side's stunning second-half comeback against Roma on Tuesday.

Portugal international Fernandes said afterwards there had been "a lot of lies" reported about his relationship with Carrick.

The 32-year-old rejected the notion there had been "clear-the-air talks" between the pair - something which had been confirmed by club sources.

"I think his actions, the way he's played and how he dealt with even retaking the penalty and frame of mind he was in for that, tells [you] everything," Carrick said.

A half-time speech, a retaken penalty - and a win to save Carrick's job?

Carrick refused to discuss the detail of his conversations with Fernandes following the Bournemouth loss, but says discussions are part of everyday life at Carrington.

"There are always conversations, and bits going on," he said. "It's acknowledging when things are going well and what we need to improve on.

"Sometimes it's individually, sometimes it's [a] group. What's actually said in that discussion, I'll keep that to myself, but it's pretty clear we've moved in a good direction.

"Bruno's commitment is undoubted for me in terms of what he brings to this team and this club."

It is anticipated United's powerbrokers will assess the managerial situation after Sunday's Premier League game against Aston Villa at Old Trafford.

Carrick accepts he does not know what will happen but he will be aware that only one victory in nine games â against Ipswich in August â is not good enough. The victory over Roma must be the start of a recovery.

"While we can be really pleased with elements of the performance on Tuesday night, we must absolutely know there is so much more to come from our team," he wrote in United's matchday programme.

"We must be ready to show that we can back up Tuesday's victory and begin to create the momentum to give ourselves something to build on after the international break."

The grim reality of United's present position was made clear by Nottingham Forest's 3-1 victory over Manchester City. That result means that Carrick's side will spend the international break in the relegation zone if they do not beat Villa.

#842. Liverpool considering Verbruggen move - Sunday's gossip

Liverpool are considering a move for Brighton keeper Bart Verbruggen, Bayern Munich remain in talks with Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha's camp and Tottenham midfielder Conor Gallagher is being monitored by rival Premier League clubs.

Liverpool are weighing up a move for Brighton and Netherlands keeper Bart Verbruggen, 24, amid doubts over the future of Brazil international Alisson Becker, 34, whose contract with the Reds expires next summer. (Football Insider), external

Bayern Munich remain in talks with Rio Ngumoha's camp after initial contact earlier this year and hope Liverpool's 18-year-old England winger could be a transfer option in the summer window. (Christian Falk), external

Liverpool have a strong interest in Brighton's highly rated Croatia centre-back Luka Vuskovic, 19, as they step up their search for a successor to Netherlands defender Virgil van Dijk, 35. (Daily Briefing), external

Chelsea and Liverpool are both interested in 21-year-old Brentford and Senegal left-back El Hadji Malick Diouf. (4-4-2.ch - in German), external

Crystal Palace, Everton and Leeds United are monitoring Tottenham midfielder Conor Gallagher, although Spurs are unlikely to let the 26-year-old England international leave. (Football Insider), external

#841. See Tiger Woods & Ex Elin Nordegren’s Reunion With Son Charlie

Tiger Woods reunited with his ex-wife Elin Nordegren as their 17-year-old son Charlie signed a contract committing to play golf at Florida State University.

Tiger Woods and Elin Nordegren are not ones to putt around when it comes to family milestones.

The former couple reunited on Nov. 6 to watch their 17-year-old son Charlie Woods sign his commitment contract to play golf for Florida State University following his high school graduation.

Tiger and Elin—who also share 19-year-old daughter Sam Woods—wore the Tallahassee-based school's signature maroon colors and were joined by the model's longtime boyfriend Jordan Cameron and their kids Arthur Cameron, 7, Zeta Cameron, 3, and Freya Cameron, 2, who also rocked Seminoles merch.

Charlie currently plays for The Benjamin School in North Palm Beach, Fla., and stands at 21st in the American Junior Golf Association rankings.

And his parents have been by his side at every step of his high school athletics career. In fact, Tiger, 50, and Elin, 46, were on hand last November to support Charlie as his team clinched the Florida High School Athletic Association Class 1A State Championship.

The duo, who divorced following Tiger's 2009 cheating scandal, also came together in February to watch the teen receive his championship ring at an awards ceremony.

“Having the relationship that I have now with her is fantastic,” Tiger—who is now dating Vanessa Trump—told Time magazine in 2015. “She’s one of my best friends. We’re able to pick up the phone, and we talk to each other all the time. We both know that the most important things in our lives are our kids.”

It's also been tee-rific for Tiger to watch his kids take a swing at golf. In recent years, the PGA Tour champion has played in tournaments with Charlie, and even had Sam join them as a caddie in 2023.

“For me to have both of my kids inside the ropes like this,” Tiger told the Golf Channel at the time, “and participating in and playing and being part of the game of golf like this, it couldn’t have been more special for me.”

To see more sports stars with their equally athletic kids, keep reading...

Michael Jordan, Jeffrey Jordan and Marcus Jordan

Considered by many to be the greatest basketball player of all time, it didn’t come as a surprise that the Chicago Bulls alum's sons, Jeffrey Jordan and Marcus Jordan, sought to follow in his footsteps. After shooting hoops in high school, Jeffrey went on to play in college at both the University of Illinois and University of Central Florida, eager to step out of his dad’s shadow.

“I guess I’m not the top one or two or three or four players in my state,” Jeffrey told The Washington Post in 2005, “but I want to show that I can play here and that I'm not just a name.”

Marcus also played basketball during his own studies at UCF, crediting his dad for helping him chart his own path.

“He was giving me tips and pointers whenever I had questions and stuff like that,” he told The Gainesville Sun in 2011, “but really he was just telling me to be focused and work hard every day, because eventually it will pay off.”

LeBron James, Bronny James and Bryce James

Bronny James (born LeBron James Jr. on born Oct. 6, 2004) played high school basketball for Chatsworth Sierra Canyon in the San Fernando Valley before graduating to the University of Southern California.

While the NBA schedule has often kept LeBron from being able to attend a full slate of his son's games, he went to great lengths to watch Bronny in action. In fact, he once chartered a plane on an off-day to catch Sierra Canyon play against his own alma mater, St. Vincent-St. Mary in Akron, Ohio.

"To go watch my son play...and also versus my alma mater," LeBron told reporters, "it's a pretty surreal, come-full-circle, unbelievable thing."

In June 2024, Bronny was drafted to the Los Angeles Lakers, making him and LeBron the first father-son duo to play in the NBA at the same time.

As for LeBron's younger son Bryce James? He started playing college basketball for the University of Arizona in 2025.

Also helping to make up the Sierra Canyon all-star squad? Zaire Wade, the eldest son of retired Miami Heat star.

"You've got to embrace it," Zaire, who transferred there in December 2019 from Florida, told Yahoo! Sports about the unusual amount of attention being paid to his team. "There are cameras on us wherever we go. There has been a lot of attention on me my whole life, but this is crazy. This is another level."

However, Zaire—unhappy with the lack of playing time he ended up getting—announced on Instagram In April 2020 that he'd be transferring to Brewster Academy in Wolfeboro, Fla.

Zaire was the 10th pick in the 2021 NBA G League draft, joining the Salt Lake City Stars. He went on to play for Cape Town Tigers of the Basketball Africa League before signing with the of the ASEAN Basketball League in April 2024.

The retired football star has a daughter who may be able to leave him in the dust by now. After all, Cha'iel Johnson is a track and field star who competed in the 2017 AAU Junior Olympics at 12, winning the girls' 800-meter run.

She ran for St. Thomas Aquinas High School in Florida, before joining the University of Kentucky athletics team.

The NBA Hall of Famer's third-eldest child, who measures up at 6-foot-10, played college basketball for UCLA before being sidelined with a heart condition that required surgery.

After missing out on his 2018-19 season with the California-based school, he transferred to Louisiana State, where there's a 900-pound bronze statue of Shaq outside the LSU Basketball Practice Facility in honor of its famous alum.

After graduating from LSU, the basketball star joined the NBA G League Ignite, a developmental basketball league in the NBA G League, in 2022.

Shaq's 6-foot-2 daughter (pictured here with her brother Shareef O'Neal) announced her LSU enrollment in 2020 to join her sibling in playing college basketball for the school.

"One of the most difficult decisions for a person my age to make, is the jump from high school to college," she shared at the time. "Although I don't fully know what's ahead of me, I am ready for the challenge. I never imagined myself saying this, but I am excited to say that I have decided to commit to being a student athlete at LSU along side my brother Shareef O'Neal. I am Sooooo grateful to spend my next 4 years as a Tiger."

She then transferred to Texas Southern University's basketball program as part of their 2021-2022 team.

The eldest daughter of two-time NBA All-Star played basketball alongside fellow NBA star scion Izela Arenas, daughter of Gilbert Arenas, during her studies at Sierra Canyon.

"I went to Michigan State under coach Tom Izzo," Randolph told the Los Angeles Times in December 2020. "He was a dog. Just hard. The boys you can be a little rough with. The girls, they have you wrapped around your finger. The girls look at you, 'Dad, I'm trying.' You have a special spot for the girls."

MacKenly said she'd beaten her dad three times in one-on-one, quipping, "He doesn't play any defense."

The 6-foot-3 son of the NFL Hall of Famer committed to Florida Atlantic University in 2019 as a preferred walk-on. Terique played basketball for most of his life before switching to football as a teen. He got his post-high school playing career off the ground at Contra Costa Community College before transferring.

After his college football career, Terique signed with the San Francisco 49ers' practice squad.

The Sierra Canyon graduate started all four years and won two state titles. He played college ball for Vanderbilt, before signing a two-way contract with the Los Angeles Lakers in 2022.

After a brief stint on the NBA G-League affiliate the South Bay Lakers, Scotty Jr. signed a two-way contract with the Memphis Grizzlies in 2024.

The former Chicago Bulls star and five-time NBA champion is a lot of things—and a dad is one of them.

His son Dennis Rodman Jr.—or DJ—played basketball and football at Corona del Mar High School in Newport Beach, Calif. After graduation, he became a forward at Washington State, before transferring to University of Southern California in 2023.

"He's one of the more under-rated or unknown players in Southern California," his high school coach, Ryan Schachter, told the Orange County Register after a game in 2017.

After his college career, DJ joined Capital City Go-Go of the NBA G League in 2024.

Though Dennis' son DJ followed his footsteps into basketball, his daughter Trinity Rodman carved her own path in the world of soccer. After the COVID-19 pandemic canceled her freshman season with the Washington State Cougars, she went professional and joined Washington Spirit in 2021 and United States women's national soccer team in 2022.

In 2024, Trinity won Olympic gold as part of Team USA at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

It's only fitting that golfing's GOAT has a kid who's got mad skills on the course. Charlie Woods made his televised-golf debut at the age of 11 alongside his dad at the 2020 PNC Championship.

When asked if he had been working on his swing ahead of the father-son outing, the 15-time major champion said, "I haven't put in any time. I don't really care about my game. I'm just trying to make sure that Charlie has the time of his life and is able to enjoy all of this.''

#839. Tottenham set to complain to Pro Ref after Bogle escapes red card

Roberto De Zerbi post-match interview - Leeds v Spurs

Tottenham are set to submit a formal complaint about the decision not to send off Jayden Bogle for his challenge on Mathys Tel during the defeat by Leeds.

Bogle, 26, escaped any punishment despite catching Spurs forward Tel on the back of the ankle with his studs in the first half of Saturday's game.

It is understood Tottenham believe Bogle should have been sent off and will write to refereeing body Pro Ref to seek an explanation as to why the incident did not result in a dismissal.

The challenge was reviewed thoroughly by the Video Assistant Referee (VAR), but referee John Brooks was not sent to the pitch-side monitor, meaning Bogle escaped any punishment.

Former Premier League assistant referee Darren Cann said the Leeds defender was "fortunate" not to be dismissed.

"Bogle's challenge meets the criteria for serious foul play as he endangers the safety of an opponent," Cann told BBC Sport. "He can consider himself lucky to still be on the pitch."

By the time play resumed, there were less than nine minutes of the first half remaining and Tottenham's momentum - and composure - were fading quickly.

Roberto de Zerbi's side never appeared to recover from the incident and, after the break, were outworked and outplayed by the home side.

Nevertheless, the Italian - perhaps buoyed by his side's recent rise up the table - refused to pinpoint Spurs' failings on the referee's decision.

"We deserved to lose the game in the second half and didn't play like we can," he told TNT Sports. "It's a journey for us because we can learn from this game.

"I am sorry for the performance in the second half - we didn't play like a top team. We didn't have the right character and physicality in the second half."

Okafor downs Tottenham to earn Leeds first win since September

Okafor the difference despite Van Hecke defiance - Leeds v Spurs ratings

Tottenham's defeat at Leeds was the first time they had lost a Premier League game since September

When the PA system at Elland Road confirmed there was a VAR check in progress, it seemed only a matter of time before Bogle would be shown a red card.

The Leeds defender was full-blooded in his pursuit of the ball from Tel and seemed certain to follow in the footsteps of Crystal Palace forward Jean-Philippe Mateta, who was sent off for a similar challenge against Spurs last weekend.

What was strange about the situation, though, was that at no point did Brooks make his way to the pitchside monitor to review the incident.

It meant the entire four-minute review was conducted solely by those in the VAR hub at Stockley Park.

"They've said no red card, and this will create debate," former Tottenham midfielder Michael Brown told BBC Radio 5 Live.

And because Brooks had not initially cautioned Bogle, the defender escaped the incident without any punishment.

"I have big confidence in the referee. Nothing changes if he goes to the monitor," said De Zerbi. "If they didn't take the right decision I don't know. We have to keep the eyes on the performance where can improve."

Early in the second half, Tottenham's frustration - seemingly stemming from the decision not to dismiss Bogle - came to a head when defender Pedro Porro and De Zerbi himself were booked simultaneously following a challenge by the Spanish defender.

De Zerbi described the decision to caution Porro as "incredible" after what had transpired during the first half.

"I was surprised on the yellow card for Pedro Porro because it was clear," the Italian told BBC Match of the Day. "The potential red card, I couldn't say.

"We have full confidence in the referee and VAR. I cannot say nothing more."

Bogle was certainly very lucky to escape even a booking.

The foul happened in strange circumstances. Bogle was positioning his body to challenge Tel with his right foot, and in trying to plant his left foot he stood on the ankle of the Spurs player.

At full speed it looked innocuous, which is probably why referee Brooks chose not to show a card after giving the foul.

Once the slow-motion replays were looked at it became apparent that the nature of the contact on Tel was very ugly, with the twist of the ankle.

It could easily have resulted in the VAR, Tony Harrington, sending Brooks to the pitchside monitor for an on-field review for a red card.

Harrington spent far too long looking at the replays, probably feeling he had more time while Tel received treatment. But longer reviews only tend to cause doubts about process.

Harrington eventually told Brooks: "I'm confirming the on-field decision of no red card. There's a lack of speed going into the challenge and he's stepping into the tackle. Confirming a reckless challenge."

A reckless challenge is a yellow card, but the VAR is unable to intervene and advise that Bogle should be booked.

Something else Harrington said is important - "stepping into the challenge".

It does not mean a player cannot be sent off, but this is far less likely to result in a VAR review for a red card because such challenges naturally come with less force.

How about comparisons with Mateta's VAR red card against Spurs last week?

There is an argument that Mateta, who was booked on-field, made less forceful contact on the ankle of Micky van de Ven. Yet it is the nature of the challenge that is crucially different.

Mateta made a lunging, stretching tackle with studs leading, the kind generally considered to come with a higher degree of force and potential danger to the opponent.

That said, and even though Bogle was not really making a challenge, the nature of the contact means many may feel there should have been a VAR review for a red card.

#837. Raya, Pickford and Wales' search for a new keeper

Arsenal's David Raya, Jordan Pickford of Everton and new Wales call-up Joe Duncan have all benefitted from non-league loans

David Raya had a loan spell at Southport before winning the Premier League with Arsenal, while Jordan Pickford spent time with Darlington and Alfreton Town on his way to a European Championship final and two World Cup semi-finals with England.

A non-league apprenticeship, it seems, can help a goalkeeper reach great heights.

That appeared to form part of Craig Bellamy's thinking when he announced his Wales squad for this month's Nations League matches against Norway and Portugal.

The one new name was Joe Duncan, a 20-year-old goalkeeper on loan at National League side Southend United from Bristol City.

Born in Bristol, Duncan was involved with Jamaica's youth set-up prior to committing to Wales, earning two under-21 caps before his surprise first call-up to the senior squad on Wednesday.

Wilson returns as Wales call up uncapped Duncan

His ascension to the higher echelons of the game has come sooner than expected, but he won't be thrown in for a debut in Oslo next weekend against Erling Haaland and company.

Instead, given Wales' dearth of goalkeeping options, Bellamy wants to take a closer look at some prospects for the future.

"You have to start somewhere as a goalkeeper, you have to learn your trade," the Wales head coach says.

"I love goalkeepers playing lower leagues, especially development goalkeepers, the ones who are looking to push through, because they [non-league players] are going to bump you and ask questions of you.

"Maybe you get over-protected the higher you go but, in those leagues, I think we quite enjoy watching those games because you're not getting anything. It's perfect, the way I see it, for a young goalkeeper.

"He's not someone who's always been on our radar because he hasn't been available to us. I have to be honest, everything I've seen with him at Southend, I really like."

It helps that Southend's manager is one of Bellamy's best friends from his playing days, former Newcastle and West Ham team-mate Kieron Dyer.

"Kieron loves [Duncan] and I respect his view on football," Bellamy says. "His IQ on the game is one of the best I've been involved with."

Bellamy has been to watch Duncan play for Southend but kept a low profile, so as not to distract the young keeper.

"That was the same week [England manager Thomas] Tuchel was watching PSG in the Champions League, so the world's different, but enjoyable," the ex-Wales captain grins.

Bellamy rummages further down the leagues than most of his international coaching peers because, quite simply, he has to. There's not much out there in terms of Welsh goalkeepers.

During his squad announcement on Wednesday, the former Liverpool and Manchester City forward described his current first-team regulars Karl Darlow, 36, and Danny Ward, 33, as "old".

It was a playful description, but his point was a serious one - where is Wales' next generation of keepers?

Everton reserve Tom King and Sheffield United's Adam Davies have usually been third choice behind Darlow and Ward but neither is playing for their club and, at 31 and 34 years old respectively, they are approaching the latter stages of their careers.

That means Bellamy has had to widen his search for successors. As he wryly notes himself, it is a far cry from Tuchel's situation with England, pondering whether to stick with Pickford or give another opportunity to Leeds United's James Trafford, who at 24 years old has already cost clubs nearly Â£100m in transfer fees.

Burnley paid a portion of that sum when Bellamy was working at Turf Moor as Vincent Kompany's assistant boss.

"You've got to earn your stripes. I've seen it with Traffs, who had really good loans with Bolton before he came to us," he says.

"We paid a lot of money for him but if we didn't do it then we were going to miss him."

Bellamy cannot delve into the transfer market to bolster Wales' goalkeeping ranks, which he describes as "an area where we're lacking at the moment".

What he can do is look far and wide â and sometimes in unexpected places â in his search for a future number one.

As Raya, Pickford, Trafford and others have shown, there is no shortage of examples to follow as Duncan plots his route to the top.

#836. Daily briefing: Toothbrush zaps bacteria to clear plaque

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Paediatrician Annie Andrews, a Democrat, won a US Senate seat in South Carolina in a surprise victory on 3 November. Democrats had not won a Senate seat in the state since 1998.Credit: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty

The US mid-term elections won the Democratic party power in both chambers of the US Congress, raising hopes that lawmakers will now push back against disruptions to science introduced by the administration of Republican President Donald Trump. Democratic majorities in both the House and Senate will give the party the power to craft legislation that counteracts Trump’s science agenda. But the President could still veto these bills, since Democrats don’t hold more than two-thirds of seats in either chamber. The results have also brought a wave of scientists and medical professionals into political office. “The nerds strike back,” says Shaughnessy Naughton, president of the political fundraising group 314 Action.

A new manual toothbrush can destroy bacteria by generating its own electrical charge, rather than relying on friction alone. The brush’s bristles are made from a polymer that researchers stretched and heated to obtain its piezoelectric form — meaning it generates a charge when deformed. During brushing, the bending bristles release charges that create highly reactive forms of oxygen in nearby saliva. These damage bacteria cell membranes, the team says. When the bristles relax, the material reabsorbs the charges, ready to go again.

Two new studies analysing more than 4,700 ancient human genomes have identified the possible origins of Celtic and Germanic languages and found migrations that might have dispersed their speakers around Europe. The findings could explain why Germanic languages such as English and Dutch are so widespread, whereas Celtic languages such as Welsh and Gaelic are concentrated to a few million people in northern Europe.

Three people with drug-resistant epilepsy saw the number of seizures they had per month fall by more than 90%, after gene-laden viruses were infused into their brains as part of an early-stage clinical trial. The treatment was targeted to the small patch of brain tissue responsible for each participants’ seizures. The virus carried a gene that made neurons in that area sensitive to clozapine, a drug that activates the gene therapy, which in turn helps to suppress the abnormal electrical activity associated with seizures. The participants didn’t experience any serious side effects, but long-term use of clozapine might bring cardiovascular risks and other problems, say researchers.

Reference: New England Journal of Medicine paper

A genetics lab in Shanghai has handed almost all control over to a team of robots guided by artificial-intelligence agents. The robotic arms in the ‘self-driving’ lab can operate more than 20 types of instrument, complete thousands of operations in a single project and see through experiments that involve synthesizing and sequencing DNA, among other tasks. The system, called ‘AutoDNA’, uses a simple human prompt to design and execute experiments. While it’s running, human hands are required only to refresh reagents and service hardware.

Health information distributed as part of a randomized clinical trial can unintentionally reshape social relationships, as demonstrated by a trial in rural Honduras. Researchers found that the intervention — which involved being provided with information about child and maternal health — affected people’s friendships, financial relationships and whom they went to for health advice. In villages where only a few people received the information, overall connectivity decreased, whereas it increased in places where the intervention covered the majority of households. (Nature News & Views | 6 min read)

When NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins launched on a SpaceX capsule to the International Space Station last month, she became the first Black woman to command a crewed space mission. Sian Proctor, the first Black woman to pilot a spacecraft (on a private SpaceX mission in 2021) reflects on how commercial spaceflight is increasing access and how Watkins’s accomplishment might help lead us to a future in space that reflects the people on Earth.

Space.com | 11 min read (free registration required)

Research into Parkinson’s disease has historically focussed on the brain, and the processes that lead to the death of dopamine neurons the disorder causes. But this research hasn’t yet pinpointed a genetic component of the disease in most people, leaving its underlying trigger unknown. Now, some researchers are investigating environmental factors that could contribute to disease onset, and others have found evidence that changes to proteins in the gut could precede symptoms in the brain.

Within a decade, humanity will know whether artificial-intelligence tools will enable “radical abundance” or “society being torn apart”, says computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton — who won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2024 for his work in developing tools for understanding the neural networks that underpin AI. #834. Olympian Gabby Thomas Reacts to Wedding Reception Being "Destroyed"

Olympic gold medalist Gabby Thomas detailed her Cabo wedding to Spencer McManes, sharing why she didn’t let a “destroyed” reception ruin their special day.

Gabby Thomas didn't let rain on her wedding day stop her from sprinting down the aisle.

A week after the Olympic gold medalist married her boyfriend Spencer McManes in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico, she shared sweet details about the beachside celebration, revealing that her reception was completely ruined by a storm.

In a Nov. 5 Instagram Reel, Thomas—who began dating McManes in 2022—shared footage of white linen-covered tables with black and gold place settings being pelted by rain, writing, “When your entire wedding reception gets destroyed minutes before it starts.”

But Thomas and McManes didn’t let some rain, well, rain on their parade.

“But it doesn’t cross your mind once all night,” the 29-year-old continued over clips of her dancing the night away with her loved ones and her now-husband inside a ballroom. “Because you had the best day of your life.”

In fact, as the track and field athlete wrote in a Nov. 5 Instagram post alongside a video compilation of her wedding day, “Gave up on perfection and focused on being in the moment together.”

Along with having her “favorite people” by her side, Thomas—who wore a stunning corseted white lace gown—said “I do” to running toward forever with her “best friend.”

And while the newlyweds had to overcome the hurdle of a storm, the moment they tied the knot on the beach was better than any gold medal.

“It had been raining all day,” Thomas recalled to Vogue in an interview published Nov. 5. “But right as our ceremony began, the rain cleared, and a vibrant rainbow appeared behind us just as I reached the altar.”

Before she got to the finish line, the sprinter slowed to a walk down the aisle with her parents by her side, describing the moment as “grateful, excited, and completely anchored.”

With her grandfather officiating the ceremony on the sand and her loved ones watching on as she and McManes exchanged vows, Thomas felt “overwhelmed with love.”

Ultimately, the Olympian is only relaying her wedding back with gratitude.

“I feel like the luckiest person in the world,” she shared. “Not just because rain is good luck, but because the people in that room made it the best day of our lives. There wasn’t a single second where we weren't smiling, dancing, or celebrating. We’re just so grateful.”

And while sharing photos from the white-veiled occasion in a Nov. 6 Instagram post, Thomas put it simply, “The most beautiful day with the love of my life. 10.30.26 forever & always.”

#833. Messi makes history with MLS Golden Boot

Messi retired from international football with Argentina earlier this year

Inter Miami forward Lionel Messi has become the first player in MLS history to win the Golden Boot in consecutive seasons.

The eight-time Ballon d'Or winner scored 26 goals in 31 appearances, four clear of FC Dallas striker Peter Musa and five more than Nashville's English forward Sam Surridge.

Messi becomes only the sixth player to land the award twice, joining a list that includes former Charlton Athletic and Southampton striker Bradley Wright-Phillips.

In addition to his goals, the 39-year-old notched 17 assists over the course of the MLS season, ensuring his 43 goal contributions was also a league best for the second year in a row.

And the World Cup winner could soon make more history as he bids to become the first three-time Landon Donovan MLS MVP winner.

The former Argentina forward landed the award in 2024 as Inter Miami won the Supporters' Shield title and also in 2025 as they won the MLS Cup.

Despite Messi's magic, Miami weren't able to land top spot in the MLS Eastern Conference, with the team finishing 17 points behind Surridge's Nashville.

They will now face Columbus Crew over three games in the first round of the MLS Cup play-offs which begin later this month.

#832. EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm

The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far too great.

As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.

Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

The European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.

The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states said open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances."

But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.

The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities."

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation."

He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.

Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.

Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides."

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation."

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she said regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.

"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she said.

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.

That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.

Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.

"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann said.

Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but said it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these new products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

"If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's important to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet."

#829. Thierno Barry double fires Everton to comeback win against Coventry

The wildly optimistic Evertonian – if such a being exists – could not have envisaged David Moyes’ side fifth in the Premier League with Thierno Barry just behind Erling Haaland in the goalscoring chart when their transfer window closed in calamitous fashion. Yet there they sit, team and striker defying all expectations, following a stirring comeback against luckless Coventry.

Frank Lampard endured a torturous night against his old club as Coventry impressed but were refused two strong penalty claims. The Coventry manager felt his team were denied a third time by the video assistant referee for an apparent handball by Barry when edging Everton ahead. Replays were inconclusive. It was the dancing French forward’s second goal of the game and 10th in all competitions this season. He also delivered a fine assist for Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall as the in-form midfielder put his latest England disappointment behind him to seal victory in convincing style.

It was a landmark occasion for Moyes as he equalled the great Harry Catterick’s record of 592 games in charge of Everton. “Seeing my name alongside Harry Catterick’s is hugely humbling and I hope I can continue to add to that figure,” the Scot wrote in his programme notes. “What I really hope, though, is that I can bring trophies to the club like Harry Catterick did.” Equalling Catterick’s collection of two league titles and an FA Cup may be beyond Moyes, who is in the final year of his Everton contract and working in very different times, but what he is doing with the smallest squad in the Premier League ranks as an achievement itself.

The Everton manager said post-match: “It’s great if I can build expectations because that means we are doing well but at some point someone is going to say ‘Look at the size of their squad’ and you might have to calm down. It might catch up with us at some point but I have to say the boys are doing really well.”

Moyes’ team laboured until falling behind to Yann Gboho’s opener early in the second half. From that moment they roused themselves and showed the clinical touch and smart decision-making that eluded Coventry, but luck was also on their side.

James Tarkowski survived two penalty appeals in one go when leaping between Caleb Yirenkyi and Ethan Pinnock to clear a Coventry free-kick. The Everton captain appeared to pull the former’s hair and raise an arm towards the latter’s face. Neither the referee, Stuart Attwell, nor the VAR, Timothy Wood, considered the hair-pull had met this season’s higher threshold for excessive force. Last season Tarkowski would have been sent off.

Lampard said: “The rules are fine. It’s not a red card and I kind of get that, but the rule remains it’s a foul so I felt it was a foul.” Coventry were denied a second penalty claim when Taiwo Awoniyi went down under a challenge from Vitalii Mykolenko. “Taiwo is on the line of the box and it is a penalty,” said Lampard. “I thought it was a penalty by the time Myko’s knee was in the back of Taiwo’s knee.”

Coventry finally, deservedly, got a break when benefiting from some abysmal Everton defending to take the lead. The influential Jack Rudoni was involved with a pass into Gboho who, with the aid of a deflection off Tarkowski, easily held off Merlin Röhl, Harrison Armstrong and Jarrad Branthwaite before poking a shot past the unsighted Jordan Pickford.

Less than 10 minutes later, and to general astonishment, Lampard’s team were behind. Tyler Dibling had been quiet on his first league start of the season but was involved in the Everton equaliser with a dangerous cross from the right. Coventry failed to clear and when Mykolenko swept in a cross at the second attempt Barry, showing good strength to hold off Jay Dasilva, beat Carl Rushworth with an emphatic header.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The French striker soon reached double figures for the campaign when bundling home Tyrique George’s delivery to the far post. Dasilva made a mess of his attempted clearance and headed the ball against Barry – his hand, possibly – before it spun past Rushworth and over the line.

There was no questioning the legitimacy of Barry’s next goal involvement. The confident striker split the Coventry defence with a superb pass into Dewsbury-Hall, who ended his disappointing day on a high by racing clear and beating Rushworth with a precise finish inside the keeper’s near post.

Moyes called Barry’s display “fabulous”. He expanded: “Haaland’s worried about him catching him now! I don’t see many young centre-forwards scoring loads of goals in the Premier League. He’s settled down a bit more now. His language, his understanding and his communication is much better as well. Obviously he’s working hard to get in those positions to score. I’m really pleased for him.”

#827. Scottish roundup: Naderi fires Rangers past St Mirren to keep pressure on Celtic

Rangers win 2-0 to go one point off top spot

Aberdeen slump to 4-0 defeat against Hibernian

Rangers banished their recent away day blues with a solid 2-0 win at St Mirren.

Draws against Dundee and Hearts in their last two Scottish Premiership games away from Ibrox had blemished their title challenge, but Derek McInnes’s side were determined to leave Paisley without a mark on them.

The in-form striker Ryan Naderi scored with a soft penalty after 18 minutes before the returning skipper, Dan Neil, added a second just after the hour mark with a deflected strike to extend Rangers’ unbeaten run in all competitions to 12 games.

Rangers moved to within one point of the leaders, Celtic, having played the same number of fixtures, albeit Celtic can restore their four-point lead if they beat Kilmarnock at home on Sunday before the international break gives them another breather.

The Aberdeen manager, Stephen Robinson, insists he will face the challenge head on as his side go into the international break in real trouble at the wrong end of the table.

Hibernian started the evening three points behind Robinson’s side, but a dominant second-half performance in a 4-0 victory at Pittodrie allowed the Edinburgh club to overtake their hosts in 10th place on goal difference.

The hosts showed promise early in the game and the Hibs keeper Raphael Sallinger saved well from Jack Milne, who also hit the bar for Aberdeen before Jamie McGrath’s 25-yard strike found the target. Aberdeen went all-out in search of an equaliser, but quickly fell 2-0 behind to Callum Wright, sparking calls for Robinson’s head from the home support. Further strikes from Thibault Klidjé and Nicky Cadden completed the rout.

Robinson said: “It’s really, really disappointing, there’s no hiding away from it. It was an unacceptable performance and an unacceptable result. We haven’t taken our chances – Hibs had five or six chances and took four of them – [and] that’s always the difference in football. We got the result we deserved.

“It’s a difficult situation, difficult for myself, the players and the club. I will keep fighting until told otherwise. We have to be better than that, that’s not acceptable. We have to get players who want to fight and try to get us out of this situation.”

Jim Goodwin, the home manager, hit out at the decision to award the penalty that cost Dundee United dear in a 1-1 draw against Motherwell at Tannadice.

The referee, Ryan Lee, had initially given a free-kick for offside in the early stages of the game. However, he was then advised by the VAR, Andrew Dallas, to have another look at an incident where Tawanda Maswanhise had gone down in the United box under a challenge by the home skipper, Dylan Tait. After checking the pitchside monitor, the referee pointed to the spot with the Motherwell captain, Lukas Fadinger, tucking the penalty away.

The hosts ultimately salvaged a point thanks to Jesse Randall’s goal but Goodwin insisted his side should have had all three. “It’s a poor decision for me,” he said. “I know it’s going to be subjective and people will have their own opinions on it, but I don’t know what Dylan Tait is meant to do.” Unsurprisingly, the Motherwell manager, Alfred Johansson, disagreed with Goodwin’s assessment, saying: “He’s on the ball and gets down from a tackle, and it’s a penalty.”

Simo Valakari was thrilled to give St Johnstone supporters a 2-1 victory over Dundee to celebrate after recent Perth struggles against their Tayside rivals.

Josh Campbell headed the home side in front after five minutes. The substitute Joe Westley replied early in the second half after a mix-up between the keeper Ross Sinclair and Cheick Diabate. Kai Fotheringham, on his first Premiership start for St Johnstone, netted a deflected winner on 72 minutes.

#825. Championship roundup: Birmingham go top, Cardiff stun Burnley from 4-1 down

Jay Stansfield earns Birmingham 2-1 win against Swansea

Cardiff stage remarkable fightback to beat Burnley 5-4

Jay Stansfield grabbed a late winner to fire Birmingham top of the Championship with a 2-1 win against 10-man Swansea.

Stansfield struck three minutes from time after a Christoph Klarer own goal had cancelled out his first-half opener for Birmingham.

“It’s great to be at the summit with everything we’ve been through and the whole journey,” said Birmingham’s manager, Chris Davies, said.

Cardiff came from 4-1 down to snatch a dramatic 5-4 win against Burnley in a second successive goal-fest in the Welsh capital.

Cardiff had seen a 3-0 lead wiped out by West Ham to drop two points in midweek, but it was their turn to come from behind here as Burnley’s miserable season continued.

The visitors opened the scoring when a hopeful punt forward from Lucas Pires allowed Andreas Hountondji to go through on goal and slide the ball past Nathan Trott.

Burnley doubled their lead 10 minutes later after great work on the left from Jaydon Banel. The ball came to Marcus Edwards on the edge of the box and he fired through a sea of bodies to beat Trott.

The hosts pulled one back before the break when Rubin Colwill’s goalbound effort bounced off Ollie Tanner and in but Krystian Bielik restored Burnley’s two-goal advantage before Alex Robertson diverted Aaron Ramsey’s cross into his own net to make it 4-1.

Yousef Salech – who had come off the bench less than two minutes before – began the comeback when he slotted home in the 65th minute and Jack Moylan made it 4-3 from the penalty spot with 15 minutes to go.

Salech headed his second goal of the game to level the scores in the 82nd minute with Robertson curling in a 30-yard wonder goal to secure the most unlikely of wins four minutes in time added on.

The Burnley manager, Fabio Celestini, said: “I can understand if there is fragility at 1-0, but it cannot happen at 4-1. It’s very difficult to accept the situation. Normally you don’t need to score four or five times to win a game, but that’s the reality.”

“It’s a very memorable day,” said the Cardiff manager Brian Barry-Murphy. “From the moment we got the second goal, I felt as though we became a very dangerous team, and the players’ belief was very evident.”

Jack McGlynn and Ben Wilmot scored as Stoke hit back to beat Portsmouth 2-1 and maintain their impressive form. Tyrese Shade put Portsmouth in front after six minutes with a lovely bending finish, but Stoke turned a tame first half around to make it five away wins in a row. McGlynn capitalised on goalkeeper Nicolas Schmid’s failure to hold on to a cross before Wilmot headed home a rebound.

“That is the first time we have won five on the bounce away from home since 1947,” said the Stoke manager, Mark Robins. “That just shows what an achievement it is.”

A magnificent display by Watford goalkeeper Federico Ravaglia denied Middlesbrough top spot as they were held to a 0-0 draw at Vicarage Road.

Middlesbrough drew a blank for the second time in four days as they rued the absence of top scorer Will Lankshear with a hamstring injury .

Middlesbrough’s head coach, Kim Hellberg, said: “I’m very angry and disappointed because with all those chances created, all those beautiful attacks we had, it’s disappointing we didn’t win the game.”

Scott Parker is still waiting for his first win as West Ham manager after a 2-1 defeat at spirited Blackburn.

West Ham dominated possession but ultimately paid for profligacy early in the second half. Andri Gudjohnsen headed in his 10th league goal of the season and Dapo Afolayan’s powerful strike doubled the Rovers advantage 19 minutes from the end.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Joel Piroe lashed in from close range to halve the deficit and Tomas Soucek missed a glorious injury time chance as West Ham suffered their first away defeat of the campaign.

Parker said: “We’re bitterly disappointed because the result hasn’t gone our way. There are certain things that were big improvements. I’ve had one training session, 45 minutes yesterday. I see a committed group at this moment in time. A lot of work to be done but I’m looking forward to it.”

Second-half goals from Isaac Price, Jayson Molumby and substitute Felix Horn Myhre gave West Brom a 3-0 win against Millwall at the Hawthorns.

James Morrison, the West Brom head coach, said: “One of our strengths is the energy and running power and we just outran them and played some nice football”

Lewis O’Brien’s first goal of the season earned Wrexham a 1-1 draw and prevented Wolves going top. Wolves have never won at Cae Ras but Adam Armstrong’s strike after 25 minutes suggested they might register a history-making victory. Instead, O’Brien equalised for Phil Parkinson’s side two minutes later though the visitors still extended their unbeaten run to six matches.

Wrexham co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney were in attendance for only this seventh league meeting between the sides in 102 years and first since 1988. Parkinson said: “It’s always very uplifting for the people who work at the club, the staff and the players when Rob and Ryan come over. The crowd too is uplifted with the owners being in town.”

Bristol City fans turned on Michael Skubala as Norwich made it nine goals in successive away victories with a 5-0 win at Ashton Gate.

Philippe Clement, the Norwich manager, said: “We are growing by the week. I am seeing boys becoming men, with clear signs of evolution from so many of our young players. That’s what we need if we are to get to where we want to be. The players are hungry and full of desire.”

Glen Kamara’s late goal gave QPR a 2-1 win over Lincoln City at Loftus Road. Richard Kone’s 11th-minute header put the hosts ahead before Dom Jefferies’ equaliser. Rangers endured a largely frustrating second half, but their persistence was rewarded in the 80th minute when Kamara thumped in his first goal since joining the club on a season-long loan from Rennes during the summer.

Jordan Thompson’s stunning volley secured Graham Alexander’s first win as Preston manager as his team shocked Southampton 1-0 at Deepdale.

Thompson won the match with a ferocious strike from outside the box in the 33rd minute and Preston held out for a vital three points.

Substitute Matty Godden’s 79th-minute goal ended Charlton’s run of 11 league matches without victory as they defeated Sheffield United 2-1 at the Valley.

On Friday night, Derby’s manager, John Eustace, handed all the praise to his group of players after they came from behind to earn their first home victory of the season with a 3-1 win against Bolton.

Derby were heading for a third straight defeat when Rúben Rodrigues notched his second goal of the season to give the Bolton a half-time lead. The home fans booed the players off and then back on to the field after the break, which clearly had an effect when Ryan Nyambe equalised with his first goal in more than 300 career appearances just 39 seconds after the break. Jack Robinson put the hosts in front three minutes later before Rhian Brewster sealed a first win since September with his first of the season in stoppage time.

#824. Here's What to Gift the Maximalist Friend Who Already Has Everything

A fellow maximalist shares niche beauty, fashion, fragrance, and accessory finds your most extra friend may not know about yet.

Do you have a friend who literally has it all? While shopping for a minimalist has its own struggles, you don't know agony unless you're looking for a gift for the maximalist in your life whose apartment is simply filled with stuff. And I know because I'm that friend (and so is every shopping writer in existence).

Knowing your friend well enough to know exactly what to gift them is good advice in general, but it's especially good advice for the maximalist. You have to know what they already have; that's all on you. As a fellow maximalist, what I can help you with in your gift-shopping journey is to give you recommendations on products that they probably want, but won't buy themselves. We're talking niche, colorful, and unique products across categories that we simply know they'll love and want.

Whether it's a beauty oracle deck your witchy friend who collects tarot decks won't have, or indie fashion and skincare brands they might not know exist (but will definitely be obsessed over), keep scrolling to shop my picks for the best gifts for that maximalist friend on your list.

As a maximalist, your friend would want to change their nails every one or two weeks. So why not gift them press-on nails with detailed designs that look like they just got out of a nail appointment? These nails are some of the best (and longest) you can get, with so many design options available.

In collaboration with Heaven Mayhem, OUAI just launched an amulet perfume necklace with one of their signature scents. It features a striking black and silver pendant, a dramatic black tassel, and notes of cocoa, tonka bean, vanilla and rum.

If your maximalist bestie loves fashion, designers, a good documentary, and a chic coffee table book, Marc by Sofia is a perfect gift. This companion book to Sofia Coppola's new documentary offers a look inside Marc Jacob's life and career through conversations between them and personal photos.

Know for a fact that your maximalist friend doesn't have a red light mask? While there are so many masks to choose from, Skin Gym's LED face mask stands out for its 10-minute treatment time and options of red (630nm), blue (465nm), and near-infrared (830nm) lights to help reduce the appearance of fine lines, smooth blemishes, and more.

Your maximalist friend definitely loses their gloves every single winter. I know it because I am her. So, get them these adorable (and cozy) knit gloves from Kurt Geiger, which feature a fuchsia ribbed knit, a rainbow Paddington embroidered badge, and a brown branded leather tag patch.

If you're looking to gift an actual sustainable and chic bag that'll last for years and isn't made of plastic, this cactus leather tote bag from Santos by Monica—with its delicious red colorway, unique geometric shape, and magnetic closure—is the only right choice (in my biased opinion).

Clinique's viral iconic shade Black Honey just got a bedazzled makeover for the holidays. The limited-edition, crystal-coated case will stop anyone in their tracks while you're reapplying.

If your maximalist friend is on the witchy side, they might have a giant collection of tarot and oracle decks. And yet, they might not have this first-of-its-kind (and unique) beauty oracle deck created by an aesthetician and Human Design expert that's perfect for every intuitive beauty lover.

Every maximalist needs at least one extra phone case—whether they just want to change the design any given day or they lost their other one. You can't go wrong with Wildflower cases, and this pop-star-approved one features a bold black star set against a sparkling crystal rhinestone backdrop.

Weird girl approved! Snif always delivers quirky and unique scents, and this pink bottle is no exception. The Lychee Lacquer is a surprisingly bright, fruity, and floral smell, with notes of lychee, nail polish accord, rose, jasmine absolute, vanilla, and musk.

Is there such a thing as too many accessories? This vintage-inspired mulberry silk bandana scarf features a trendy olive green shade, playful polka dot details, hand-rolled edges, and hand-stitched finishing.

If you're worried about gifting skincare to your maximalist friend who has it all, we recommend opting for indie and new brands. Lazy Skincare has only been around for a year, and it already has devoted fans (myself included). Their hero product is Double Duty, a serum-moisturizer duo that's formulated with skin-firming red carmellia extract, smoothing bakuchiol, hydrating silver ear mushroom, and more.

While you could just stumble into a vintage shop and get anything from there for your maximalist friend, why not also get them a new style alongside it? Damson Madder is that brand for anyone who loves their clothes to have an interesting shape while still being wearable—and this trench coat is simply a perfect example of that.

For your maximalist friend who loves a good board game, mahjong might be the next hobby they'll get into (if they aren't into it already). This high-quality tile set is one-of-a-kind, with its intricate designs, vibrant colors, floral motifs, and chic tortoise back.

#823. Steinmeier in China: A major state visit in uncertain times

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is traveling to China on a state visit in a period of political and economic uncertainty. Germany is seeking alternative partners in the region but also wants good ties with Beijing.

Eight years have passed since Frank-Walter Steinmeier's last trip to China. Since then, the relationship between China and Europe has changed significantly. The German president plans to spend several days touring China before concluding his visit in Beijing, where he will meet with China's leaders.

His visit comes just as the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee is convening for its plenary session, a major annual event that foreign dignitaries usually avoid when timing their visits.

The focus of the president's five-day trip will be "Germany's diverse and complex relations with China, as well as the challenges involved," his office said in a statement. In addition to sites of cultural exchange, the itinerary will also include a visit to a Volkswagen plant in Hefei.

The automotive industry, in particular, illustrates the dilemma facing Germany's China policy. China is one of the most important markets for German automotive and machinery manufacturers, as well as for the chemical industry. At the same time, state-supported overcapacity in China is putting pressure on European manufacturers.

Not only that. Germany and Europe are dependent on China for raw materials and technologies, which means they are increasingly seeking out alternative partnerships.

Steinmeier was once an advocate of the policy of "change through trade" — the idea that other countries could be persuaded to become more democratic with the leverage of global trade — which has few adherents left in Germany today.

Now he must now pursue a tougher European line in Beijing. Caught between partnership and competition, Europe leaders recently managed to reach an agreement: Imports of plug-in hybrid vehicles from China are to be scaled back.

"That was a concrete step, but it can only be the beginning," said Michael Laha, an expert on China at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) in Berlin.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Coinciding with Steinmeier's state visit to China, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is traveling to the Indo-Pacific with business representatives. His visit to Japan, Singapore and South Korea will focus on competitiveness, technological upheavals, defense cooperation and critical raw materials. Merz is visiting companies and attending important regional economic conferences in Tokyo and Seoul.

The dual trips are Berlin's attempt to send a twofold message: While the chancellor is "deliberately strengthening Germany's partnerships in the Indo-Pacific at a time of global upheaval," according to Laha, the president is seeking dialogue with Beijing at a time when Germany and Europe are recalibrating their relationship with China.

"This joint trip sends a very well-coordinated message to the Chinese that we remain committed to the partnership but at the same time are taking steps to reduce risk," said Laha, before adding that this is a difficult balancing act that also allows China to save face.

While Merz will be accompanied by a large economic delegation, Steinmeier will be traveling to China with representatives from German culture, politics, and academia. Mikko Huotari, director of the China Institute MERICS, is also expected to be part of the delegation — even though Beijing has imposed sanctions on the institute. "The fact that he is coming along sends a clear message to the Chinese side that we do not approve of the sanctions," said Laha.

In 2021, the EU imposed sanctions against several Chinese party and regional officials, as well as an organization accused of serious human rights violations and oppressing the Uyghur minority. It was the first time such sanctions had been imposed on China since the Tiananmen Square massacre in 1989, and Beijing did not take kindly to them. In response, the Chinese government imposed entry bans and other sanctions against European politicians, scholars, and institutions, including MERICS.

Laha did not expect human rights to play a major role in the German president's trip. Steinmeier is considered a pragmatist when it comes to China policy. As foreign minister, he distanced himself from his predecessor Joschka Fischer, a critic of China, and even criticized Chancellor Angela Merkel when she hosted the Dalai Lama.

On the subject of Ukraine, Steinmeier is likely to be more direct and raise the issue of China's role in the conflict. "Beijing is clearly on Moscow's side," said Laha. In Berlin, however, officials are convinced that China can do more to persuade Russia to engage in serious negotiations and find a solution to the conflict.

Steinmeier may make this clear in his speech at Peking University on Thursday. Germany has "long viewed China's emergence with respect and goodwill," read a statement from the president's office. Today, however, the focus is less on China's continued rise and more on how it uses its growing power.

"If the president points out that Russia used its power to attack a sovereign state, he could be alluding to another regional connection: Taiwan," said Laha. That could be seen as an appeal to Beijing to assume more responsibility for the regional and international order.

To conclude his visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership in Beijing. Talks are planned with President Xi Jinping, whom he has known for nearly two decades, as well as with Premier Li Qiang and the chairman of the National People's Congress, Zhao Leji.

The trip marks the culmination of Steinmeier's focus on Asia during his second term in office. Since then, he has deliberately sought to forge close ties with partners in the region and has advocated for greater diversification. Now China, which is Germany's most important and most challenging partner, will come to its own conclusion.

#821. NWSL playoffs: Cooper’s extra-time penalty sends Kansas City through as Utah stun San Diego

Michelle Cooper strikes in extra time to lift Current

Kansas City extend unbeaten home record with 1-0 win

Seventh-seeded Utah Royals upset San Diego Wave

Michelle Cooper converted an extra-time penalty to give the Kansas City Current a 1-0 victory over Angel City on Sunday in the quarter-finals of the National Women’s Soccer League playoffs.

The fourth-seeded Current will face the winner of Sunday’s quarter-final between top-seeded Gotham FC and No 8 Seattle Reign FC in next weekend’s semi-finals.

Kansas City, the only NWSL team to finish the regular season unbeaten at home, extended that run into the postseason.

Angel City goalkeeper Angelina Anderson made five saves in regulation. Four minutes into extra time, Kansas City defender Izzy Rodriguez sent in a corner kick. Before the ball went over the crossbar, Current defender Kayla Sharples went to ground near the goal line after contact with Anderson and midfielder Ary Borges. Kansas City were awarded a penalty, which Cooper converted.

The teams combined for 25 fouls in a physical encounter. Fifth-seeded Angel City collected three yellow cards in regulation, the first in the 13th minute when Sveindís Jónsdóttir slid into Gabrielle Robinson from behind as the Kansas City defender shielded the ball near her end line.

Borges was booked in the 58th minute after catching Vanessa DiBernardo with her cleat as they challenged for a ball in the air. In second-half stoppage time, Maiara Niehues clipped Cooper’s heel and knocked off her cleat. Kansas City’s only yellow card went to Temwa Chawinga in the 114th minute.

The seventh-seeded Utah Royals earned their first playoff victory with a 1-0 upset of the second-seeded San Diego Wave in Friday night’s NWSL quarter-final.

Cloé Lacasse delivered a pinpoint low cross to Kiana Palacios, who took a touch before firing home the game’s only goal in the 30th minute. It marked the first time Utah had led San Diego in any competition this season.

Royals goalkeeper Mandy McGlynn made four saves to record her sixth clean sheet of the season.

“Unbelievable, it’s just everything you could hope for,” McGlynn said. “I’m like in shock, no words can describe this feeling.”

The Royals snapped a four-match winless streak and will travel to face either the third-seeded Washington Spirit or sixth-seeded Portland Thorns in the semi-finals. Washington host Portland in Sunday’s remaining quarter-final.

Both teams were missing key players. San Diego midfielder Kimmi Ascanio was unavailable with a thigh injury, while Utah midfielder Mina Tanaka, initially listed as questionable with a hamstring injury, was ruled out.

The Wave were held scoreless despite dominating possession (62% to 38%), shots (16-8) and shots on target (5-2).

San Diego entered the match on a seven-match unbeaten run but have now lost four consecutive playoff matches.
